sources.entry: Complexity and Strategy: interesting perspective on complexity and flexibility with really good examples (e.g. Google Apps Suite vs. Microsoft Office).

summary.title: Complexity and Strategy
summary.one_liner: Software cost curves tend to turn convex as feature interactions accumulate, so strategy should isolate essential complexity rather than expect new technologies to flatten it.
takeaways: Feature cost for large systems tends to grow with feature interactions (essential complexity), giving a convex cost curve.
New technologies and frameworks often give an initial productivity boost on small codebases, but the curve shape does not change as the product grows.
Walking away from existing complexity (as OneNote did) can enable innovation, while embracing it can create a defensible moat, such as Office file formats.
Isolating complexity into simpler, shareable components is preferred over building one ever-larger core engine that serves all apps.
summary.summary: The author, a former Microsoft Office development leader, models software enhancement as a curve of aggregate functionality against aggregate cost and argues that large systems usually follow a convex curve. He illustrates this with examples from FrontPage's Preview view, Word's table feature estimates versus PowerPoint, OneNote's decision to leave Word's codebase, and the porting of Office to new platforms. The essay then applies the model to new technologies, Google Apps competition, the move to web apps and the file-format moat, and the debate with Bill Gates over a central core engine. It is a long first-person essay with no code, relying on experience-based reasoning rather than measured data.
